title: End-to-End Optimization of Partial Fault Tolerance in Neutral-Atom Arrays
authors: Stefano Veroni, Aydin Deger, Andrew J. Daley
abstract: Fault-tolerant (FT) quantum computation offers a pathway to quantum advantage, but its realization is hindered by its significant overhead. The partially FT "STAR" architecture reduces the cost of universal computation at the price of relaxing FT requirements for non-Clifford operations, increasing exposure to hardware noise. Therefore, maximizing its performance and applicability demands careful co-design with the underlying hardware. In this work we investigate the co-design of the STAR architecture with neutral-atom platforms, connecting the underlying atomic physics to logical error modeling and application-level performance. At the physical level, we identify a favorable noise bias in $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ Rydberg gates, and show how it can be enhanced through error-selective pulse optimization. At the logical level, we identify an intrinsic error suppression mechanism, yielding vanishing logical coherent noise in leading order. Detailed circuit-level simulations of surface code implementations show more than an order of magnitude reduction in logical error relative to previous estimates. As a concrete target application, we focus on the Fermi-Hubbard model with periodic boundaries, for which we design a simulation circuit particularly suited to early implementations. We quantify the resource tradeoff of partially and fully FT approaches to gate synthesis, with the former showing approximately an order of magnitude reduction in state-injection depth, and an even larger reduction in Clifford resources. Comparing with classical and fully FT approaches, we identify regimes where partial fault tolerance provides both lower overheads and lower error rates. In our estimates, this is accessible with moderate error rates $p\sim 10^{-3}$ and a few thousand qubits, underlining that for these types of problems, partial FT approaches provide a compelling pathway to early quantum advantage.
summary: This paper investigates optimizing quantum computation using a partially fault-tolerant (pFT) architecture tailored for neutral-atom arrays. By co-designing the STAR protocol with ${}^{171}	ext{Yb}$ Rydberg gates, the authors achieve significant reductions in logical error rates and resource overhead. They conclude that pFT offers a practical and advantageous route for achieving quantum advantage in simulating models like the Fermi-Hubbard model with current hardware capabilities.
main_problem: The primary challenge is realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation while minimizing the significant overhead associated with fully fault-tolerant methods.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that a partially fault-tolerant (pFT) approach using the STAR architecture offers a compelling pathway to early quantum advantage, showing significant reductions in logical error rates and resource overhead compared to full FT methods.
method: The work involves co-designing the pFT architecture with neutral-atom hardware, performing error-selective pulse optimization at the physical level, and running detailed circuit-level simulations on the rotated surface code.
model_or_system: The physical platform is neutral-atom arrays utilizing ${}^{171}	ext{Yb}$ Rydberg gates. The computational model is based on the STAR architecture, which implements partial fault tolerance for universal computation.
key_observables: Logical error rate, resource overhead (state-injection depth, Clifford resources), and the regime of advantage compared to classical/NISQ and fully FT approaches.
important_parameters: Moderate physical error rates ($p \sim 10^{-3}$) and qubit counts in the few thousand range are identified as the accessible regime for early advantage.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the partial fault tolerance provides a better balance of overhead and error rate for near-term quantum simulation tasks.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the pFT realization of rotations, the TMR encoding in the rotated surface code, the physical device operation, and a map comparing the regimes of advantage (Classical/NISQ vs. Full FT vs. Partial FT) for the Fermi-Hubbard model.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the overhead problem in FT computation to proposing the pFT STAR architecture. It details physical improvements via pulse optimization, establishes the logical error suppression mechanism, quantifies resource trade-offs, and concludes by applying the framework to simulating the Fermi-Hubbard model.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges the gap between advanced quantum information theory (pFT, surface codes) and cutting-edge experimental hardware (neutral atoms), providing concrete, resource-aware pathways for near-term quantum simulation.
